title: Using the Microscope
subtitle: Wet mounts, and how big a cell really is
subject: Biology
syllabusModule: Cells as the basis of life
syllabusDotPoints: Use calibrated microscope measurements to estimate cell size, including cell size = diameter of field of view ÷ number of cells across the field
lessonIntent: Students can prepare and observe cells, distinguish a calibrated field-of-view measurement from an image measurement, and calculate real cell size using both methods.
examSkill: Choose the method from the information given: cell size = field-of-view diameter ÷ number of cells across, or real size = image size ÷ magnification. Convert units before calculating.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, we prepare a slide and measure real cells. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: How big is it, really?
scenes.body: A cell can fill the whole field of view, yet it is microscopic. A grid and a known magnification turn what you see into a real measurement.
scenes.callout: Reading about a cell is one thing; measuring it is another.
scenes.caption: A grid and the magnification equation turn an image into a real size.

voiceover.text: Under a microscope, a single cell can fill the whole field of view. But you know it's microscopic. So how big is it, really? With nothing more than a grid and a known magnification, you can turn what you see into an actual measurement in micrometres. Today you'll prepare a wet mount of onion skin, find the cytoplasm, cell wall and nucleus, and then work out how big those cells actually are.

scenes.heading: Preparing a wet mount
scenes.body: A good wet mount keeps the specimen flat, hydrated and stained, with no trapped air bubbles.

bullets.text: Water on a clean slide; lay a thin layer of onion epidermis in it; add a drop of iodine to stain.
Lower the coverslip at an angle so air is pushed out; focus on low power first.
Cell wall: firm outer boundary. Cytoplasm: pale jelly. Nucleus: darker, stained, rounded.

scenes.callout: A dark-edged circle is usually a trapped air bubble, not a cell.
scenes.caption: Water, thin specimen, stain, angled coverslip; then find the wall, cytoplasm and nucleus.

voiceover.text: Here's the method. Place a drop of water on a clean slide. Peel a thin layer of onion epidermis and lay it flat in the drop, because light has to pass through it. Add a drop of iodine to stain it. That adds contrast, so structures stand out. Then lower the coverslip from one edge, at about forty five degrees, so air is pushed out ahead of the liquid. Trapped bubbles are dark edged circles that beginners mistake for cells. Now focus on low power first, then high power. Under the light microscope, the cell wall is the firm outer boundary. The cytoplasm is the pale jelly filling each cell. And the nucleus is a darker, stained, rounded structure. Safety note, slides and coverslips are sharp glass, and iodine stains skin and clothes.

scenes.heading: Measuring with a mini-grid
scenes.body: A calibrated field of view turns what you see into a real measurement. If several similar cells span the field, estimate one cell by dividing the field diameter by the number across.

bullets.text: Field-of-view method: cell size = diameter of field of view ÷ number of cells across it.
Example: 2.0 mm field ÷ 5 cells = 0.40 mm = 400 µm.
Image method: magnification = image size ÷ real size; use this only when measuring a magnified image.

scenes.callout: Field of view ÷ cells across gives an estimated real cell size.
scenes.caption: Cell size = field-of-view diameter ÷ number of cells across; image measurements use magnification.

voiceover.text: A calibrated field of view gives another direct way to estimate cell size. If five similar cells fit across a field that is two point zero millimetres wide, use the NESA equation: cell size equals the diameter of the field of view divided by the number of cells across it. Two point zero millimetres divided by five is zero point four zero millimetres, or four hundred micrometres. If instead you measure a cell on a photograph or screen, that is an image measurement, so use magnification equals image size divided by real size. The key is to identify which kind of measurement the question gives you.

scenes.heading: Specialised cells vary in size
scenes.body: Cells are specialised for different jobs, and their sizes vary widely.

bullets.text: Red blood cell about 8 µm; cheek cell about 60 µm.
Onion epidermal cell 200–300 µm long; a nerve cell can be over a metre.
Measure several cells and use the mean to improve reliability.

scenes.callout: State results with units and sensible significant figures.
scenes.caption: From 8 µm red blood cells to metre-long nerve cells: size relates to function.

voiceover.text: Are all cells the same size? Not even close, which is why the syllabus says measure a variety of specialised cells. A red blood cell is about eight micrometres across. A human cheek cell, about sixty. An onion epidermal cell can be two hundred to three hundred micrometres long. And a nerve cell can be over a metre long. Measuring several different cells shows that size relates to function. And measuring several cells of the same kind, then taking the mean, improves the reliability of your estimate. Always give the unit, and a sensible number of significant figures.

footer.text: measure several cells, then take the mean

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Wet mount: a specimen in a drop of liquid under a coverslip, keeping it hydrated and clear.
Stain: a dye such as iodine or methylene blue that adds contrast.
Magnification: how many times larger the image is than the object (objective × eyepiece).
Micrometre (µm): one-thousandth of a millimetre; 1 mm = 1000 µm.
Mini-grid: a grid of known square size on the stage, read in real micrometres.

scenes.caption: Wet mount, stain, magnification, micrometre, mini-grid.

voiceover.text: Five terms. A wet mount is a slide where the specimen sits in a drop of liquid under a coverslip, keeping it hydrated and clear. A stain is a dye, like iodine or methylene blue, that adds contrast so structures stand out. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object, and it's the objective lens times the eyepiece lens. A micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre. And a mini grid is a grid of known square size on the stage, which reads in real micrometres.

scenes.heading: Estimate cell size from field of view
scenes.question: A microscope field of view is 1.8 mm wide. About 6 similar cells fit across its diameter. Estimate the width of one cell in micrometres.
scenes.coachNote: Use cell size = field-of-view diameter ÷ number of cells across, then convert millimetres to micrometres.
steps: Known: field-of-view diameter = 1.8 mm; cells across = 6.
Formula: cell size = field-of-view diameter ÷ number of cells across.
scenes.caption: 1.8 mm ÷ 6 = 0.30 mm = 300 µm.

voiceover.text: Here's the field-of-view calculation. The field is one point eight millimetres wide and about six similar cells fit across it. Use cell size equals field-of-view diameter divided by the number of cells across. One point eight divided by six is zero point three zero millimetres. Convert that to micrometres by multiplying by one thousand, giving three hundred micrometres. Because the cells do not usually line up perfectly, report it as an estimate.

scenes.heading: The multiply trap
scenes.body: Trap: 'To find the real size, multiply the image size by the magnification.'
scenes.secondary: Divide. The image is the enlarged view, so real size = image size ÷ magnification. And never divide a stage-grid reading: it is already real. A cell answer below 1 µm usually means the magnification was applied twice.
scenes.callout: Image measurement: divide. Grid reading: no division.
scenes.caption: Real size = image ÷ magnification; a stage-grid reading is already real.

voiceover.text: Two traps here. The first is multiplying the image size by the magnification to get the real size. The image is the enlarged view, and the real cell is smaller, so you divide. The second is the opposite mistake, dividing a stage grid reading by the magnification. That grid was already magnified along with the cell, so its reading is already real. If you get a cell smaller than one micrometre, smaller than most bacteria, you've probably applied the magnification twice.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Against a stage grid of 100 µm squares, a cheek cell spans two-fifths of one square. What is its real width? How wide would it appear at ×400?
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause: is the grid reading real or magnified?
answerSteps: The stage grid reads in real micrometres, so no division.
Answer: 40 µm wide, appearing 16 mm across at ×400 ✓
scenes.caption: Grid reading 40 µm is real; at ×400 it appears 16 mm wide.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Against a stage grid of one hundred micrometre squares, a cheek cell spans two fifths of one square. What's its real width, and how wide would it appear at times four hundred? Pause, and decide, is the grid reading real or magnified? OK. The stage grid reads in real micrometres, so no division. Zero point four times one hundred is forty micrometres. Then forwards, forty times four hundred is sixteen thousand micrometres, or sixteen millimetres.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Wet mount: water, thin specimen, stain, coverslip at an angle, low power first.
Wall: firm boundary; cytoplasm: pale jelly; nucleus: darker and stained.
Field-of-view method: cell size = field-of-view diameter ÷ number of cells across.
Image method: magnification = image size ÷ real size; divide a magnified image measurement by magnification.
Measure several specialised cells and take the mean; include units.
scenes.finalPrompt: Before calculating: field of view, or magnified image?
scenes.caption: Prepare, identify, measure: grid readings are real, image readings get divided.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Prepare the specimen carefully, identify the structures you can actually see, then choose the measurement method from the information given. For a calibrated field of view, cell size equals the field diameter divided by the number of cells across it. For a magnified photograph or screen measurement, magnification equals image size divided by real size, so divide the image measurement by magnification. Convert units before you calculate and include units in the answer.
